title: Chapter 12 — Cooking: Ranges and Cooktops
intro: Gas, electric, and induction — the fuel conversation and the demo that converts.

sections.title: The Fuel Conversation
sections.content:
Gas, electric, or induction is not a preference question — it is a home infrastructure question. Does the home have a gas line? What amperage is the electrical circuit? Is the customer open to induction?

Start with what the home supports. Then discuss what the customer prefers. Recommending a gas range to someone with only electric service creates a problem, not a sale.

sections.title: Induction Is the Demo That Converts
sections.content:
Most customers who resist induction have never seen it work. The boiling water demo — where induction boils water in under two minutes versus eight for electric — converts skeptics into buyers.

If your store has a working induction display, use it. If it does not, advocate for one. Induction is the fastest-growing cooking technology and the demo sells itself.

sections.title: Sizes and Configurations
sections.content:
30-inch is standard. 36-inch is the step up for serious cooks. 48 and 60-inch are luxury and professional.

Slide-in versus freestanding matters for aesthetics and installation. Cooktop plus wall oven combinations offer flexibility but require more installation planning.

Know the sizes, know the configurations, and match them to the kitchen — not just the customer's wish list.

sections.title: Coaching Rule
sections.content:
When evaluating cooking knowledge, ask:

Does the salesperson verify the home's fuel source before recommending?
Can they demonstrate induction effectively?
Do they understand size and configuration options?
Do they connect cooking features to the customer's cooking habits — discovered in Step 3?
